issues.legal_issue: A state rule may prefer public-sector entities in granting leases for minor minerals where the preference serves conservation and efficient exploitation and the application criteria permit comparison of applicants.
material_facts: The amended rule gave state-owned companies or corporations preference when leases were granted for specified varieties of granite in private land, but did not exclude private applicants.

The application requirements sought information about an applicant’s identity and business, mining dues, prior work in the area, the quantity sought, the intended period of quarrying and transport, and the intended use of the mineral.
The stated purpose of the policy was to conserve valuable granite resources and ensure their proper and efficient use.
The applicants sought leases to quarry minor minerals; the earlier rule contained no promise that the prior policy would continue unchanged.
issues.conclusion: The preference provision was valid. It was within the State’s rulemaking power, had a rational connection to conservation and prudent exploitation, and was not unconstitutional for want of guidelines. It did not amount to an exclusive reservation circumventing the statutory reservation procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, read with the public-interest declaration in Section 2, permits rules regulating grants of leases for minor minerals in furtherance of conservation and prudent exploitation. State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone supports restricting private exploitation where public-sector exploitation is considered the best means of achieving that purpose. The application information required under Rule 3 and Appendix X supplies relevant factors for comparing applicants, and preference operates where competing applications are otherwise equal on those factors. Section 17A(2) concerns exclusive reservation of an area and does not apply to a preference that leaves private applicants eligible. Under Section 24A, consent of the occupier is required only for entry into a building or an enclosed court or garden, not for the ordinary mining entry authorized by a lease. The former rule made no promise that would attract promissory estoppel, and the State may alter its policy in response to its view of conservation needs.

rule.if: lease_rule_challenge and minor_minerals_sought and public_entity_preference and conservation_objective and comparative_application_information

predicates.lease_rule_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a state rule governing the grant of mineral leases.
predicates.minor_minerals_sought: The applicants seek leases to quarry minerals treated as minor minerals for the purpose of the proceeding.
predicates.public_entity_preference: The rule gives public-sector entities preference in granting leases while leaving other applicants eligible.
predicates.conservation_objective: The preference is adopted to conserve a valuable mineral resource and promote its prudent exploitation.
predicates.comparative_application_information: The application process requires information relevant to comparing applicants and their proposed use of the mineral.

issues.definition: When a challenged lease rule concerns minor minerals, gives public-sector entities a conservation-based preference, and permits comparison using relevant application information, the preference rule is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A state rulemaking power confined to regulating grants of minor-mineral concessions does not authorize control of sales or prices after minerals have been extracted.
material_facts: The challenged rules authorized the State, its officers, or a state-owned company or corporation to regulate sales of quarried granite and similar decorative or ornamental rock.
The rules also authorized those bodies to fix minimum sale prices.
The State directed a state-owned company to regulate those sales, relying on conservation of granite resources as the purpose.
The rules applied to minerals after quarrying and therefore concerned their subsequent sale and sale price.
issues.conclusion: The rules regulating sales and fixing minimum prices after extraction were beyond the State’s rulemaking power and were invalid. The related government orders were invalid to the extent that they prescribed or implemented those rules.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15(1) and 15(1A) authorize State rules regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases, and other mineral concessions for minor minerals, and matters connected with those grants. Section 15(1A)(o), concerning other prescribed matters, remains confined to that subject and does not authorize regulation of the sale of minerals already mined or their sale price. Section 18 places a conservation duty on the Central Government but does not confer on the State the power to control post-extraction sales or prices. Such control cannot be justified as a means of conserving the mineral resource after excavation.

rule.if: state_mineral_rule_challenge and minor_mineral_regulation and minerals_extracted and (sale_control or minimum_price_control)

predicates.state_mineral_rule_challenge: A party challenges a state rule made in relation to minor minerals.
predicates.minor_mineral_regulation: The rule purports to regulate minor minerals under the State’s delegated rulemaking authority.
predicates.minerals_extracted: The minerals covered by the rule have already been quarried or otherwise extracted.
predicates.sale_control: The rule authorizes a state body to control the sale of the extracted minerals.
predicates.minimum_price_control: The rule authorizes a state body to fix a minimum price for the extracted minerals.

issues.definition: When a challenged state rule for minor minerals controls sales or minimum prices after extraction, the post-extraction control rule is invalid.
